# Working on remote machines: `ssh`, `scp`, `rsync` and `tmux`

Big data rarely lives on your laptop. You work on a server or a cluster: a computer in a machine room that you reach over the network, with far more cores, memory and disk than yours puny laptop/desktop. Everything you have learned so far works there too, because they will 99% of the time run linux. And you give it commands through a bash shell just like the bash shell on your laptop. The tools below get you there, move the files, and keep your jobs alive.

(These examples need an account on a remote machine. Replace `user@server` with your own login.)

## `ssh`: log in to another machine

`ssh` ("secure shell") gives you a shell on another machine over the network. Everything sent between the two machines, including your password, is encrypted.

```bash
ssh user@server          # log in; the prompt is now on the server
ssh user@server "df -h"  # run one command there and come back
exit                     # leave the server (or Ctrl+D)
```

After `ssh` connects, you are typing into a shell on the server, and `pwd`, `ls`, `htop` and the rest refer to *that* machine. Check which one you are on by the prompt or with `hostname`.

Let's try it on Moriah, the HUJI cluster. Its login machine is called `moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il`. That name is registered with DNS and refers to an ip address.

Computers on a network find each other by number, the **IP address** ("internet protocol"), four numbers from 0 to 255 such as `132.65.10.20`. Numbers (just like phone numbers) are hard for people to remember, so the internet keeps a giant phone book, the **DNS** ("domain name system"), that turns names into numbers (just like the phone book on your iPhone/android). Read the name from right to left, from the biggest part to the smallest: `il` is Israel, `ac` its academic institutions, `huji` the Hebrew University, `cs` its computer science department, and `moriah-gw` one machine there (`gw` for "gateway", the way into the cluster). When you type `ssh kapelner@moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il`, your computer first asks a DNS server for the number and then connects to that number. You can do the lookup yourself:

```bash
host moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il     # prints its IP address (nslookup does the same)
```

So the phone number is "132.65.180.50" but luckily you don't have to remember it. Okay let's try connecting. Replace `kapelner` with your own login:

```bash
ssh kapelner@moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il #if you're at home, this hangs...
```

Why does it hang? Because the computer moriah is not reached directly: you first hop through a server named "bava" and then reach the main server "moriah", and `-J` ("jump") does the hop in one command. 

```bash
ssh -J kapelner@bava.cs.huji.ac.il kapelner@moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il
```

You will be asked for a one-time code (from the authy/authenticator app or SMS you registered with the university) and then your password.

Why two hops? Security. A machine that anyone on the internet can reach is attacked all day long: automated programs try common passwords on every address they can find. So the university's firewall lets the outside world reach only a few **gateway** machines, such as `bava`, which are kept small, up to date and closely watched. The cluster, with its valuable hardware and everyone's data, accepts `ssh` only from inside the network. An attacker must break into the gateway first, and that is the one machine the administrators watch most closely. This arrangement is common, and the gateway is often called a **jump host** or **bastion**. The second login is then encrypted all the way from your computer to `moriah-gw`, so even `bava` never sees what you type there.

From inside campus, this should work:

```bash
ssh kapelner@moriah-gw.cs.huji.ac.il
```

A few things to do once you're inside of a new computer:

```bash
hostname                         # the cluster's name, not your laptop's
cat /etc/os-release              # which Linux, and which version
whoami                           # your username on the remote machine
id                               # your user number and your groups
```


`id` prints a line such as

```
uid=12345(kapelner) gid=100(users) groups=100(users),2051(statlab)
```

Linux does not really know you by name but by a number, your **user ID** (`uid`). The name in parentheses is only a label for it. You also belong to one or more **groups**, each with its own number (`gid` is your main group, `groups` lists all of them). Groups are how a shared machine hands out permissions (see lec02 for permissions discussion). We are "statlab"! Cool...

```bash
free -h                          # how much memory
nproc  --all                     # how many cores this machine has
systemctl show user-$(id -u).slice -p CPUQuotaPerSecUSec -p MemoryMax # am I being metered here?
```

This means we're not being metered on memory but we are tightly metered on CPU. All your processes on this login node together may use 300 ms of CPU time per second of real time. That's 30% of one core. All your programs running at once share the same 30%. Even when the machine is idle, you can't go above it. Let's see what this means:

```bash
time python3 -c "sum(range(10**7))"
```

The total time is ~3.33x the user (CPU) time.

Let's continue poking around in our new computer at this machine:

```bash
uptime                           # how busy it is: compare the load average to nproc
```

Over the last 1, 5, 15 min what # of cores were being used on average?

```bash
who                              # who are those n users? Are my friends here with me???
who | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u | wc -l #how many unique users are there really?
df -h ~                          # how much space do I have in my personal directory
                                 # We will eventually have shared space for the class - 
                                 # I'll explain that when the cluster people set it up
sudo -l                          # security check first then ... fails - I'm just a peon... just like you guys
exit                             # back to your own computer
```


## `scp` and `rsync`: copy files between machines

`scp` ("secure copy") is `cp` across the network, sent through an encrypted `ssh` connection. The remote side is written `user@server:path`, and the colon is what says "this is on the server":

```bash
scp results.csv user@server:~/data/     # your computer to the server
scp user@server:~/out/model.pkl .       # server to here (. : this folder)
scp -r results/ user@server:~/          # -r : a whole folder
```

`rsync` ("remote sync") does the same job better for anything big or repeated. It compares both sides and sends only what is missing or changed, so a second run of a large copy takes seconds, and an interrupted one can be resumed:

```bash
rsync -av data/ user@server:~/data/     # -a : keep folders, dates; -v : talk
rsync -avz data/ user@server:~/data/    # -z : compress while sending
rsync -avP data/ user@server:~/data/    # -P : progress, keep partial files
rsync -avn data/ user@server:~/data/    # -n : dry run, only show the plan
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## The trailing slash matters
`rsync -av data/ dest/` copies the *contents* of `data` into `dest`. Without the slash, `rsync -av data dest/` creates `dest/data`. The same is true on the destination side. When in doubt, add `-n` first.
:::

## `tmux` on the server: keep your work alive

This is what `tmux` from Lecture 2 is for. Start it *on the server*, right after you log in, and run your long job inside it:

```bash
ssh user@server
tmux new -s analysis             # a session on the server
Rscript long_job.R               # start the long job
# Ctrl+B then D : detach
exit                             # log out; the job keeps running
```

Close your laptop, lose your Wi-Fi, go home. Later:

```bash
ssh user@server
tmux ls                          # analysis: 1 windows ...
tmux attach -t analysis          # back where you left off, output and all
```

The session lives on the server, not on your laptop, so it survives a dropped `ssh` connection as well as a deliberate logout.

`nohup` from Lecture 2 also works for this but `tmux` is the safer choice where the job's terminal belongs to the `tmux` session, which never goes away when you log out. Neither one comes with a guarantee. A remote server is not your machine: the system administrator is in control and can kill anything they want. They may set the server to kill all of your processes when you log out, `tmux` included, or kill any job that runs too long or uses too much memory on a shared login machine. Read your server's rules, and on a cluster put long jobs in the "scheduler", which is what it is there for. We will return to the scheduler later (on moriah they use a program called SLURM).

Make it a habit: whenever you `ssh` in to do something that takes more than a minute, start or attach to a `tmux` session first.


# PostgreSQL ("postgres")


## Logging in to the database

Check that the postgres server is running and that you can log in. The command is to run postgres is `psql`:

```bash
psql -c "SELECT version();"      # a line starting with: PostgreSQL 18
psql
```

Now we get a different prompt. We're inside the database program. Commands in bash don't work here. We use another language here. Recall our discussion on `awk` and recall this command

```bash
awk -F, 'NR>1 {n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}' covid.csv #### don't run, we're not in bash anymore
#        ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
#        awk's own proprietary language which people call
#        "awk", "awk program", "awk script"
```

So too PostgreSQL has its own language. In fact it's an internationally standardized language called "Structured Query Language" (SQL, pronounced "sequel" or "S-Q-L").

Review of history from last lecture: SQL was standardized in 1986 by ANSI, the American standards body, and in 1987 by ISO, the international one. It grew out of SEQUEL, a language IBM researchers designed in the early 1970s; the name was shortened to SQL because "SEQUEL" was already a trademark, but the old pronunciation stuck. The standard has been revised many times since, most recently in 2023. Every major database speaks SQL, so what you learn here in the dialect we're using (postgres) carries over to other dialects MySQL, SQLite, Oracle, SQL Server and the rest. 

Thus, SQL is like the "English" of data (the default communication protocol) of which there are a few dialects with very little differences e.g. British "clever" = American "smart", British "trousers" = American "pants".

Note: each dialect adds its own extensions. So the postgres backslash commands such as \timing and \copy are not SQL at all.

Notice that you gave neither a username nor a password. The username is easy: when you do not give one (with `-U`), `psql` uses your Linux username. If you do not name a database, it also connects to the one with your username. Why no password? Your setup created a database user (Postgres calls it a **role**) with the same name as your Linux user. When `psql` connects to a server on the *same* machine, it does not go over the network. It uses a special file called a **socket**, and through a socket the server can ask the operating system which Linux user is on the other end. You already proved who you are when you logged in to the computer, so the server takes the operating system's word for it and lets you in as the role with your name. This is called **peer authentication**, and it is set by a rule in the server's configuration file `pg_hba.conf` ("host-based authentication").

Connections from other machines arrive over the network, where the server has no way to ask anyone's operating system. They need a password or a key. So a database on another computer will always ask you to prove who you are.

## Using Postgres on Moriah

Log into moriah and try `psql`. You will most likely get `command not found`. A cluster serves hundreds of users who need different programs, and often different versions of the same program, so most software is installed side by side and switched off until you ask for it. The `module` command does the asking. First search for what is available:

```bash
ssh moriah
psql #fails
module spider postgres           # every Postgres version installed here
module spider postgres/17        # details about one version
```

`module spider` only *searches*. To actually use a version, load it:

```bash
module load postgres/17          # adds psql and friends to your PATH
which psql                       # now found
psql --version
```

A loaded module lasts only until you log out, and the next login starts clean again. To load it every time, put the line into `~/.bashrc` on Moriah, which bash runs at the start of every session. Then `source` the file, which runs it in the current shell, so you do not have to log out and back in:

```bash
echo 'module load postgres/17' >> ~/.bashrc   # >> appends; > would wipe the file
source ~/.bashrc
```

From now on Postgres is there every time you log in, and you never need to think about this whole `module` thing ever again.

Let's go back to our local computers:

```bash
exit
```
## postgres databases

What is a postgres "database"? One Postgres server holds many **databases** which in turn houses **tables** (to be explained shortly). The unit of the database is one that store data for a logical project, application or analysis. For example, a clinic's database might have patients, visits and prescriptions. These tables refer to each other (a visit belongs to a patient), and questions often need several of them at once. We will be seeing all this in good time. Grouping a project into one database pays off in four ways:

* Queries: a query can combine tables only within one database, so tables that are used together must live together.
* Names: each project has its own namespace, so two projects can each have a table called results in two different databases.
* Permissions: you can give access to someone to one database without giving access to your other databases.
* Lifecycle: you can back up a database as a unit (pg_dump lec04 > lec04.sql), copy it to another server, or delete it with dropdb, without touching the other projects.

A database is **not** a file you can see. Postgres keeps all the databases together in its own storage folder, in a format only it reads, and you reach the data only by asking the server. (Compare SQLite, a smaller database where each database *is* one file.)

By default, there are two databases already present:

```
your local Postgres server
├── postgres       (made at setup; a default place to connect)
├── kapelner       (the one named after you)
```

Which database are we in by default?

```bash
psql
```

You can read it from the default prompt "<username>=#". You can verify it and see more information here:

```sql
\conninfo
--comments go after two hypens unlike bash
```

To list the databases on the server, type `\l`:

```sql
\l
```

As you can see, I'm using databases for other projects I'm involved with.

You can live in one database per `psql` session. You can switch databases via `\c` is short for `\connect`:

```sql
\c postgres
\c kapelner
```

You use `\q` to quit and return to bash:

```sql
\q
```

We can create a database using the bash program `createdb`. We'll create one for this lecture and open postgres directly into it:

```bash
createdb lec04                   # a new, empty database
psql lec04                       # the interactive prompt; \q quits
```

Again, this database is a named, walled-off collection of tables, a bit like a folder of files. You connect to **one** database at a time (`psql lec04`), and a query can only see the tables in that one. Two databases can each have a table called `covid` without any clash. That makes a database the natural unit for one project. Make one per project, and when the project is over, `dropdb` deletes it and everything in it in a single step.


## Loading the CSV

A database table, like parquet, has **typed columns**. We state them up front and then load the file with `\copy`, which reads a file on *your* machine:

```sql
-- print how long each statement took
\timing on
-- this is a "slashed command" or a metacommand. It is not part of SQL; it is a direct psql command 
CREATE TABLE covid (
  date   date,
  county text,
  state  text,
  fips   text,
  cases  integer,
  deaths integer
); --creates a table with each column as a certain type. 
--This is a SQL command. It ends with a semicolon and can span multiple lines
-- describe a table: its columns and their types (type q to exit)
\d covid
-- list the tables
\dt
-- copies from CSV into the postgres table
\copy covid FROM 'covid.csv' CSV HEADER
```

In the `\copy` command, the `CSV HEADER` tells postgres that the first line holds column names and not data. The load takes about a second. 
NOTE: Use `\copy` and not the canonical SQL version `COPY`. `COPY` makes the *server* read the file, and the server is a different user who is not allowed into your home folder.)

NOTE: comments on the same line as metacommands break the metacommands and should not be used.

## Queries

A **query** is a question you ask the database. In SQL it is a `SELECT` statement (command), and the answer always comes back as a new little table of rows and columns. It is a read-only operation. It will not change the underlying data. 

(Other SQL statements *change* things, such as `CREATE TABLE`, `INSERT` and `UPDATE`. A query only reads.)

A query is built from **clauses**, which always appear in this order and are all optional except `SELECT`:

+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| Clause                 | What it does                                    |
+========================+=================================================+
| `SELECT ...`           | which columns ... (or calculations) to return   |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `SELECT *`             | return all the columns                          |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `SELECT DISTINCT ...`  | return each unique row only once                |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `SELECT ... AS name`   | give a returned column a name of your choice    |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `FROM ...`             | data from table ... to read                     |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `WHERE ...`            | keep only the rows that match condition ...     |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY ...`         | sort the answer by column ... smallest first    |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY ... DESC`    | sort the answer by column ... largest first     |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY a, b DESC`   | sort by `a`; break ties by `b`, largest first   |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `LIMIT ...`            | keep only the first few ... of the answer       |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+
| `OFFSET ...`           | skip that many rows first (used with `LIMIT`)   |
+------------------------+-------------------------------------------------+

The condition after `WHERE` can be built from **operators**:

+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+
| Operator                   | Meaning                                    | Example                                      |
+============================+============================================+==============================================+
| `=` `<>` `<` `>` `<=` `>=` | compare                                    | `cases > 1000`                               |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+
| `AND` `OR` `NOT`           | combine conditions                         | `state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris'`      |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+
| `LIKE` with `%`            | text pattern: `%` is any text, even none   | `county LIKE 'San %'`                        |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+
| `LIKE` with `_`            | text pattern: `_` is exactly one character | `fips LIKE '48___'` (the Texas codes)        |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+
| `IN (...)`                 | one of a list                              | `state IN ('Texas', 'Utah')`                 |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+
| `BETWEEN ... AND ...`      | in a range, ends included                  | `date BETWEEN '2020-12-01' AND '2020-12-31'` |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+
| `IS NULL`                  | the value is missing                       | `deaths IS NULL`                             |
+----------------------------+--------------------------------------------+----------------------------------------------+

SQL is **declarative**. You describe *what* answer you want, not *how* to get it: no loops over lines, no choice of which file to read first. Postgres has a **query planner** that works out the fastest way to run each query without you changing a word of it.

### Row-level queries ("detail queries" or "non-aggregate queries")

These types of queries match one output row per matching input.

Some examples with only these clauses:

```sql
-- the first 5 rows, all columns: like head
SELECT * FROM covid LIMIT 5;
-- only three of the columns
SELECT date, county, cases FROM covid LIMIT 5;
-- each state only once, in alphabetical order
SELECT DISTINCT state FROM covid ORDER BY state LIMIT 5;
-- only the rows for Harris County, Texas
SELECT date, cases FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris'
  LIMIT 5;
-- the same rows, oldest date first
SELECT date, cases FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris'
  ORDER BY date
  LIMIT 5;
-- the 5 rows with the most cases on New Year's Eve 2020 (Los Angeles first, 770915)
SELECT county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  ORDER BY cases DESC
  LIMIT 5;
-- OFFSET: the next 5, ranks 6 to 10 (Harris, Texas first, 237727)
SELECT county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  ORDER BY cases DESC
  LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;
-- ORDER BY two columns: by state, then within each state by cases, largest first
-- (DESC applies only to cases; the states stay A to Z, so Alabama's Jefferson comes first, 52339)
SELECT state, county, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31'
  ORDER BY state, cases DESC
  LIMIT 5;
-- AS: name the columns of the answer, and use the name in ORDER BY (Harris, Dallas, Tarrant)
SELECT county, cases AS total_cases, deaths AS total_deaths FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND state = 'Texas'
  ORDER BY total_cases DESC
  LIMIT 3;
-- LIKE with %, and >: counties starting with "San " with over 100000 cases (San Bernardino, San Diego)
SELECT county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND county LIKE 'San %' AND cases > 100000
  ORDER BY cases DESC;
-- LIKE with _, and <: Texas fips codes (48 then 3 characters) with under 10 cases (King 6, Loving 1)
SELECT county, fips, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND fips LIKE '48___' AND cases < 10;
-- OR: the parentheses matter, because AND is applied before OR (Dallas and Harris)
SELECT county, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND state = 'Texas'
    AND (county = 'Harris' OR county = 'Dallas');
-- IN: a shorter way to write several ORs (Clark, Nevada first, 170032)
SELECT county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND state IN ('Utah', 'Nevada')
  ORDER BY cases DESC
  LIMIT 5;
-- BETWEEN: Harris County in the first week of December 2020, both ends included (7 rows)
SELECT date, cases FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris'
    AND date BETWEEN '2020-12-01' AND '2020-12-07'
  ORDER BY date;
-- IS NULL: rows where deaths is missing (all of them are in Puerto Rico)
SELECT date, county, state, cases FROM covid
  WHERE deaths IS NULL
  LIMIT 5;
-- NOT: missing deaths outside Puerto Rico (no rows at all)
SELECT date, county, state FROM covid
  WHERE deaths IS NULL AND NOT state = 'Puerto Rico';
\q
```

Without `ORDER BY`, the rows come back in whatever order Postgres finds them, so `LIMIT 5` alone gives you *some* 5 rows, not the first 5 of anything. Add `ORDER BY` whenever the order matters.

For comparison, here are the same questions using bash with `awk` as the star of the show:

```bash
head covid.csv -n 1 
#date,county,state,fips,cases,deaths
# the first 5 rows, all columns (NR>1 skips the header line)
awk 'NR>1' covid.csv | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# only three of the columns
awk -F, -v OFS=, 'NR>1 {print $1, $2, $5}' covid.csv | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# each state only once: sort -u sorts and drops repeated lines
awk -F, 'NR>1 {print $3}' covid.csv | sort -u | head -n 5
# only the rows for Harris County, Texas
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$3=="Texas" && $2=="Harris" {print $1, $5}' covid.csv | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# the same rows, oldest date first
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$3=="Texas" && $2=="Harris" {print $1, $5}' covid.csv | sort | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# the 5 rows with the most cases on New Year's Eve 2020
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# OFFSET: tail -n +6 starts at line 6, skipping 5
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | tail -n +6 | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# ORDER BY two columns: sort with two keys, the first as text, the second as numbers in reverse
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" {print $3, $2, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k1,1 -k3,3nr | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# AS: no real equivalent, because awk output has no column names; you can only echo a header line yourself
{ echo "county,total_cases,total_deaths"
  awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $3=="Texas" {print $2, $5, $6}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k2,2nr | head -n 3
} | column -s, -t
# LIKE with %, and >: a regular expression, ^ means "starts with"
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $2 ~ /^San / && $5 > 100000 {print $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | column -s, -t
# LIKE with _, and <: in a regular expression . is one character, $ means "ends here"
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $4 ~ /^48...$/ && $5 < 10 {print $2, $4, $5}' covid.csv | column -s, -t
# OR is ||
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && $3=="Texas" && ($2=="Harris" || $2=="Dallas") {print $2, $5}' covid.csv | column -s, -t
# IN: awk has no IN, so we write out the ORs
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$1=="2020-12-31" && ($3=="Utah" || $3=="Nevada") {print $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv | sort -t, -k3,3nr | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# BETWEEN: two comparisons (dates written YYYY-MM-DD sort correctly as text)
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$3=="Texas" && $2=="Harris" && $1 >= "2020-12-01" && $1 <= "2020-12-07" {print $1, $5}' covid.csv | sort | column -s, -t
# IS NULL: the field is empty
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$6=="" {print $1, $2, $3, $5}' covid.csv | head -n 5 | column -s, -t
# NOT is !
awk -F, -v OFS=, '$6=="" && !($3=="Puerto Rico") {print $1, $2, $3}' covid.csv | column -s, -t
```


Each SQL clause has an awk counterpart:

+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| SQL                  | `awk` (and friends)             |
+======================+=================================+
| `SELECT ...`         | `{print ...}`                   |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `SELECT DISTINCT`    | `| sort -u`                     |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `AS name`            | no equivalent (no column names) |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `FROM covid`         | the file name, `covid.csv`      |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `WHERE ...`          | the pattern before the `{`      |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY ...`       | `| sort`                        |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY ... DESC`  | `| sort -r`                     |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `ORDER BY a, b DESC` | `| sort -k1,1 -k2,2r`           |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `LIMIT ...`          | `| head -n ...`                 |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `OFFSET 5`           | `| tail -n +6`                  |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `=`                  | `==`                            |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `<>`                 | `!=`                            |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `<` `>` `<=` `>=`    | `<` `>` `<=` `>=`               |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `AND`                | `&&`                            |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `OR`                 | `||`                            |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `NOT`                | `!`                             |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `LIKE 'San %'`       | `~ /^San /`                     |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `LIKE '48___'`       | `~ /^48...$/`                   |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `IN ('a', 'b')`      | `($3=="a" || $3=="b")`          |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `BETWEEN a AND b`    | `$1 >= a && $1 <= b`            |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+
| `IS NULL`            | `$6==""`                        |
+----------------------+---------------------------------+

Remember in `awk` you refer to columns by number (which is super annoying because you have to remember that `$3` is the state), and you have to tell `sort` that column 3 holds numbers (`-k3,3n`). SQL uses the names and already knows the types. 

Which is more readable? awk or SQL?


### Aggregate queries ("summary queries")

Functions such as `count(*)`, `max()`, `sum()` and `avg()` are **aggregates**: they boil many rows down to one number.

+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| Aggregate             | What it returns                                   |
+=======================+===================================================+
| `count(*)`            | the number of rows                                |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| `count(...)`          | the number of rows where the column is not `NULL` |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| `count(DISTINCT ...)` | the number of different, unique values            |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| `sum(...)`            | the total                                         |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| `avg(...)`            | the mean                                          |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| `min(...)`            | the smallest value                                |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| `max(...)`            | the largest value                                 |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+
| `stddev(...)`         | the sample standard deviation                     |
+-----------------------+---------------------------------------------------+

All of them except `count(*)` skip `NULL` values, so `avg(deaths)` is the mean of the rows where `deaths` is known.

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM covid;                                 -- 884737, the same as wc -l (minus the header)
SELECT count(*) FROM covid WHERE state = 'Texas';           -- 67002
SELECT max(cases) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris';              -- 237727
-- count(column) skips NULLs: 18761 fewer than count(*), the Puerto Rico rows with no deaths
SELECT count(deaths) FROM covid;                            -- 865976
-- count(DISTINCT ...): states (including DC and the territories) and Texas counties
SELECT count(DISTINCT state) FROM covid;                    -- 55
SELECT count(DISTINCT county) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas';                                    -- 255: 254 counties plus "Unknown"
-- sum: deaths in the whole country by the end of 2020
SELECT sum(deaths) FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31';    -- 346050
-- avg prints many decimals; round() tidies it
SELECT avg(cases) FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-12-31';     -- 6170.9710323574730354
SELECT round(avg(cases)) FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31';                                -- 6171
-- min works on dates too: the first day in the data, and Texas's first case
SELECT min(date) FROM covid;                                -- 2020-01-21
SELECT min(date) FROM covid WHERE state = 'Texas';          -- 2020-02-12
-- stddev: counties differ a lot in size
SELECT round(stddev(cases)) FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31';                                -- 23169
-- several aggregates in one query give one row with several columns
SELECT min(date), max(date), count(DISTINCT date) FROM covid;       -- 2020-01-21 | 2020-12-31 | 346
SELECT count(*), count(deaths) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Puerto Rico';                              -- 19055 | 294
SELECT sum(cases), round(avg(cases)), max(cases) FROM covid
  WHERE date = '2020-12-31' AND state = 'Texas';            -- 1770527 | 6971 | 237727
```

The Texas count is exactly 67,002 with no regular expression and no counting of the wrong column. Because each column has a name and a type, `state = 'Texas'` cannot match a county. These queries take about 60 to 90 ms: faster than `awk`, but still reading the entire table.

## Grouped aggregate queries

`GROUP BY` splits the rows into groups, here one group per state, and the aggregate is computed separately for each group, so the answer has one row per group. The `GROUP BY` clause goes after `WHERE` and before `ORDER BY`:

```sql
SELECT state, count(*) FROM covid
  GROUP BY state ORDER BY count(*) DESC LIMIT 5;            -- top 5 states
```

This is the `awk` program `{n[$3]++} END {for (s in n) print s "," n[s]}` from before, plus the sort and the `head`, in one line. There is one rule to remember. Every column after `SELECT` must either be in the `GROUP BY` or be inside an aggregate. `SELECT state, county, count(*) ... GROUP BY state` fails, because a state has many counties and Postgres cannot know which one to show. (A `GROUP BY` with no aggregate at all, such as `SELECT state FROM covid GROUP BY state`, is legal but only removes duplicates, so write it the clearer way, `SELECT DISTINCT state FROM covid`.)

The real speed-up comes next.

## Indexes

An **index** is a sorted lookup structure that the database keeps beside the table, like the index at the back of a book. Instead of reading every page to find "Harris", it looks up the entry and jumps to the right pages.

```sql
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT max(cases) FROM covid
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris';
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` shows how Postgres ran the query. Without an index you will see `Seq Scan` (a *sequential scan*: reading every row) and an execution time of about 70 ms. Now create the index and run the same `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` again:

```sql
CREATE INDEX ON covid (state, county);     -- takes about a second, once
```

The plan changes to an `Index Scan` (or `Bitmap Index Scan`) and the time drops to **under 1 ms**. The table has 884,737 rows, and the database looked at about 300 of them.

The time to answer is now almost independent of the table's size. That is the reason databases exist. The cost is paid once, when you build the index (about 1.2 seconds here), plus a little extra on every insert to keep the index up to date and some extra disk space.

## Indexes at scale

Now the same 20 lookups as in the Parquet unit, but against the 44-million-row `covid_big.csv`. Load it into a table of its own and build an index on the three columns we filter by (the load takes about a minute, the index about another minute and a quarter, and the table takes about 3 GB on disk, of which the index is 0.3 GB):

```sql
CREATE TABLE covid_big (date date, county text, state text, fips text, cases integer, deaths integer);
\copy covid_big FROM 'covid_big.csv' CSV HEADER
CREATE INDEX ON covid_big (state, county, date);
```

Then ask the same 20 questions from R, through the `DBI` package, which talks to Postgres:

```{r}
library(arrow)
library(dplyr)
library(DBI)

setwd("~/workspace/HUJI_52002_Fall_2026/scratch/lec04")

ds <- open_dataset("covid_big.parquet")
set.seed(1)
counties <- ds |> distinct(state, county) |> collect()
counties <- counties[sample(nrow(counties), 20), ]   # the same 20 random counties

con <- dbConnect(RPostgres::Postgres(), dbname = "lec04")
system.time(
  for (i in 1:20) {
    dbGetQuery(con,
      "SELECT max(cases) FROM covid_big WHERE state = $1 AND county = $2 AND date = $3",
      params = list(counties$state[i], counties$county[i], as.Date("2020-12-31")))
  }
)
dbDisconnect(con)
```

```
   user  system elapsed 
 ...        ...   0.03
```

0.03 seconds for all 20, about 1.5 ms each, compared with 19 seconds for Parquet: **roughly 600 times faster**. The index lets Postgres jump straight to the 50 matching rows instead of reading 44 million. Parquet is the better format for scanning entire columns (try adding up `cases` for the whole table: Parquet wins easily), and a database is the better tool for finding a few rows fast. Drop the big table when you are done: `DROP TABLE covid_big;`.

## The database checks your data

Try to add a row with a nonsense value:

```sql
INSERT INTO covid VALUES ('2021-01-01', 'Harris', 'Texas', '48201', 'N/A', 0);
-- ERROR:  invalid input syntax for type integer: "N/A"
```

A CSV would have accepted that line without complaint, and the problem would have appeared much later, in the middle of an analysis. A database refuses bad data at the door. Types are the simplest of its guarantees. Later you can add rules such as `NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE` and `CHECK`.

## Changing data

Fixing one value touches only the rows you name:

```sql
UPDATE covid SET deaths = deaths + 1
  WHERE state = 'Texas' AND county = 'Harris' AND date = '2020-12-31';
```

A database does not care where a row "goes": it writes the change into free space and updates its index, which takes a fraction of a millisecond. Compare that with rewriting a 35 GB Parquet file. You can also wrap several changes in a **transaction** (`BEGIN; ... COMMIT;`), and either all of them happen or none of them do. If the machine crashes halfway through, the database recovers to a consistent state.

## Using the database from the shell

You do not need the interactive prompt. `psql -c` runs one statement, and the output can feed straight back into the pipes you already know:

```bash
psql lec04 -c "SELECT count(*) FROM covid"
psql lec04 -At -c "SELECT county FROM covid WHERE state='Utah'" | sort -u
psql lec04 -c "\copy (SELECT * FROM covid WHERE state='Utah') \
  TO 'utah.csv' CSV HEADER"
```

`-A` turns off the table formatting and `-t` removes headers and footers, which leaves plain lines for `sort`, `wc` and friends. The last line goes the other way and writes the result of a query out as a CSV.

## What did you install?

Postgres is a lot of software. Add it up, with `du` ("disk usage") for the program files and the database itself for your data:

```bash
du -ch /usr/lib/postgresql /usr/share/postgresql | tail -n 1   # the program
psql -At -c "SELECT pg_size_pretty(sum(pg_database_size(datname)))
             FROM pg_database"                          # all your data
```

`du -c` adds a grand total at the end and `tail -n 1` keeps only that line. On Ubuntu the program is about 50 MB. (On a Mac with Homebrew, use `du -shL "$(brew --prefix postgresql@18)"`.) The `covid` table alone took about 63 MB with its index, almost twice the 35 MB CSV.

That is a lot of space for a program whose job is to store rows. But look at what it bought you in this unit:

- **Speed:** the same question went from scanning every row (about 70 ms here, and growing with the table) to under 1 ms with an index, and that stays true as the table grows.
- **Correctness:** typed columns refused `'N/A'` as a number, and rules such as `NOT NULL` and `UNIQUE` can refuse other nonsense when it arrives.
- **Safe changes:** single-row updates and transactions that happen completely or not at all, even if the machine crashes.
- **Many users at once:** many programs reading and writing the same tables at once without corrupting them.
- **A query language** instead of one-off shell pipelines: SQL, with joins, grouping and sorting, and a planner that picks how to run each query.

PostgreSQL grew out of research at Berkeley in the 1980s and has had decades of engineering since. Nobody would write all of that again for one analysis. That is why it is worth the space: you get it for free, and it is already installed.

## Clean up

```bash
dropdb lec04                     # delete the whole database
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it
1. Find the five counties with the highest `deaths` on 2020-12-31, as a single SQL statement (`ORDER BY` and `LIMIT`). Your first attempt will probably list counties with *no* number at all. Some rows in the CSV have an empty `deaths`, which the database stores as `NULL`, and `ORDER BY ... DESC` puts `NULL` first. Fix it with `NULLS LAST`.
2. Time the query "maximum `cases` in Harris, Texas" with and without the index (`DROP INDEX` to remove it). Then do the same with `awk` on the CSV. How many times faster is the indexed query?
3. Load the CSV again into a second table, but declare `cases` as `text`. What changes, and which of the queries above breaks or gives wrong answers? (Try `max(cases)`: as text, `'9999'` sorts after `'237727'`.)
:::
